title: Nowcasting Recession Risk in the Euro Area: A Hierarchical Bayesian Approach
text:
Official business cycle dating in the Euro Area, as carried out by the Centre for Economic Policy Research (CEPR), is inherently retrospective: recessions are announced only months after their onset. For policymakers and financial market participants who require timely assessments of macroeconomic conditions, such delays are costly. This has motivated a substantial body of research on real-time monitoring of economic activity, which broadly falls into two strands. The first, pioneered by Giannone et al. (2008) and extended by Bańbura et al. (2013), uses high-frequency indicators to track current-quarter GDP growth. The second, rooted in the work of Estrella & Mishkin (1998) and Chauvet & Piger (2008), models the binary recession state directly via probit or logit specifications.
Furno & Giannone (2024) propose a logit-based framework for nowcasting recession risk that combines sentiment and financial-stress indicators. A natural limitation of estimating such models on a country-by-country basis is that individual Euro Area member states—particularly those that adopted the euro relatively recently—may have experienced only a small number of recession episodes, leading to imprecise and unstable coefficient estimates. We address this issue by embedding the recession logit within a hierarchical Bayesian structure that allows country-specific parameters to deviate from a common distribution, thereby inducing partial pooling across geographies.
Our approach also draws on the “Growth-at-Risk” framework of Adrian et al. (2019), who emphasize the role of financial conditions in shaping the distribution of future output growth. We incorporate the Composite Indicator of Systemic Stress (CISS) of Holló et al. (2012) as a measure of financial fragility and the Economic Sentiment Indicator (ESI) as a gauge of macroeconomic expectations. The resulting model produces real-time recession probability estimates for the Euro Area aggregate and four major member states (Germany, France, Italy, and Spain), along with Bayesian credible intervals that quantify estimation uncertainty.

title: Nowcasting Recession Risk in the Euro Area: A Hierarchical Bayesian Approach
text:

title: Methodology
text: This document describes the econometric and statistical methodology used to nowcast recession risk in the Euro Area and its four main member states: Germany (DE), France (FR), Italy (IT), and Spain (ES). The framework is based on the methodology proposed by Furno and Giannone (2024), extended here to a hierarchical multi-country setting.

title: Methodology
text:
1 The Nowcasting Problem
A central challenge in macroeconomic monitoring is the timely detection of business cycle turning points. Dating committees, such as the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) in the United States and the Centre for Economic Policy Research (CEPR) in the Euro Area, officially announce recessions with a delay of several months or even years. Official quarterly Gross Domestic Product (GDP) figures are also published with a lag of several weeks and are subject to subsequent revisions.
To address these limitations, we formulate a model to nowcast the probability that a country is in a recession during the current quarter. Unlike standard forecasting models that predict future recessions over a horizon \(h > 0\) (e.g., Estrella and Mishkin (1998)), nowcasting focuses on estimating the state of the economy at the present moment \(h = 0\) (see Giannone, Reichlin, and Small (2008) and Bańbura et al. (2013)).

title: Methodology
text:
2 Model Specification
Let \(y_{i,t} \in \{0, 1\}\) be a binary indicator representing whether geography \(i\) is in a recession at quarter \(t\). The probability of recession is denoted by: \[ p_{i,t} = P(y_{i,t} = 1 \mid \mathbf{x}_{i,t}) \]
We model \(y_{i,t}\) using a Hierarchical Bayesian Logit regression. The log-odds (logit) of being in a recession is a linear function of a macroeconomic indicator and a financial indicator:
\[ \text{logit}(p_{i,t}) = \ln\left(\frac{p_{i,t}}{1 - p_{i,t}}\right) = \alpha_i + \beta_{1,i} \text{CISS}_{i,t} + \beta_{2,i} \text{ESI}_{i,t} \]
where: - \(\text{CISS}_{i,t}\) is the standardized Composite Indicator of Systemic Stress for geography \(i\). - \(\text{ESI}_{i,t}\) is the standardized Economic Sentiment Indicator for geography \(i\).

2.1 Hierarchical Structure
A key feature of our approach is the hierarchical pooling of parameters across countries. Rather than estimating independent models for each country or a single pooled model that assumes identical relationships, the hierarchical model assumes that country-specific parameters are drawn from a shared global distribution:
\[ \alpha_i = \alpha_0 + u_{0,i} \] \[ \beta_{1,i} = \beta_1 + u_{1,i} \] \[ \beta_{2,i} = \beta_2 + u_{2,i} \]
where: - \(\alpha_0\) represents the global average intercept. - \(\beta_1\) and \(\beta_2\) represent the global average effects of the financial stress indicator (CISS) and macroeconomic sentiment (ESI), respectively. - \(\mathbf{u}_i = (u_{0,i}, u_{1,i}, u_{2,i})'\) is a vector of geography-specific random effects.
We assume that the country-specific deviations are normally distributed: \[ \mathbf{u}_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{\Sigma}) \]
The covariance matrix \(\mathbf{\Sigma}\) captures the variability of the intercepts and slopes across geographies, as well as the correlations between them: \[ \mathbf{\Sigma} = \text{diag}(\boldsymbol{\sigma}) \, \mathbf{R} \, \text{diag}(\boldsymbol{\sigma}) \] where \(\boldsymbol{\sigma} = (\sigma_{\alpha}, \sigma_{\beta_1}, \sigma_{\beta_2})'\) are the standard deviations of the random effects, and \(\mathbf{R}\) is the correlation matrix.
This hierarchical structure allows for “shrinkage,” which pulls country-specific estimates toward the Euro Area average. This is particularly beneficial for countries with short sample histories or fewer recession observations, as the model borrows statistical power from the rest of the group.

title: Methodology
text:
3 Data and Variables

3.1 Target Variable: Technical Recession
Following standard convention, we define a technical recession as two consecutive quarters of negative quarter-on-quarter real GDP growth:
\[ y_{i,t} = \begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } \Delta \text{GDP}_{i,t} < 0 \text{ and } \Delta \text{GDP}_{i,t-1} < 0 \\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases} \]
where \(\Delta \text{GDP}_{i,t}\) represents the percentage growth rate of seasonally and calendar adjusted real GDP for country \(i\) in quarter \(t\).


3.2 Predictor Variables

Economic Sentiment Indicator (ESI): Sourced from Eurostat, the ESI is a composite indicator made up of five sectoral confidence indicators with different weights (industrial, services, consumer, construction, and retail trade). It serves as a timely tracker of macroeconomic sentiment.
Composite Indicator of Systemic Stress (CISS): Developed by Holló, Kremer, and Lo Duca (2012) and sourced from the European Central Bank, the CISS measures the level of systemic stress in the financial system. It aggregates indicators across five market segments (money, equity, bond, foreign exchange, and financial intermediaries) using portfolio theory to weight segments by their correlation. This captures the systemic dimension of financial stress, which has been shown to be a crucial driver of economic downside risks (Adrian, Boyarchenko, and Giannone (2019)).

Prior to estimation, both predictors are scaled (mean-centered and divided by their standard deviation) to facilitate MCMC convergence. In the production scripts the scaling parameters are computed on the full available sample (a mild look-ahead that only affects the location/scale of the predictors, not their shape); the pseudo-real-time backtest instead computes them on the training window only, so that no post-cutoff information enters the simulated nowcasts.

title: Methodology
text:
4 Bayesian Estimation and Priors
The model is estimated using Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods via the brms package in R, which interface with Stan. We specify weakly informative priors for the parameters to stabilize estimation while letting the data dominate the posterior:

4.1 Population-Level (Fixed) Effects

Global Intercept: \(\alpha_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 5)\)
Global Slopes: \(\beta_k \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 2)\) for \(k \in \{1, 2\}\)

These priors are conservative; they restrict coefficients to plausible ranges while remaining flat enough over the regions of high likelihood.


4.2 Group-Level (Random) Effects

Standard deviations: \(\sigma \sim \text{Student-}t(3, 0, 2.5)\) (truncated to positive values)
Correlation matrix: \(\mathbf{R} \sim \text{LKJ}(1)\)

These are the brms defaults used by the production scripts (new_code/recessione_CISS_ESI.R, new_code/recessione_CISS_PMI_composito.R); they are weakly informative and only regularize extreme values. The LKJ prior with \(\eta = 1\) is uniform over all correlation matrices, representing a neutral prior belief about the correlations between random intercepts and slopes. The pseudo-real-time backtest (new_code/pseudo_realtime_ESI_vs_PMI.R) instead sets the slightly tighter \(\sigma \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 2)\) and \(\mathbf{R} \sim \text{LKJ}(2)\) with adapt_delta = 0.95, for numerical stability across the many refits of the simulation; this choice affects the backtest comparison only, not the production estimates.

title: Methodology
text:
5 Inference and Out-of-Sample Evaluation
The model is fitted on training data up to a cutoff date representing the maximum available data minus 5 years. This allows us to perform out-of-sample inference on the last 5 years.
For each quarter \(t\), we compute the posterior probability distribution of \(p_{i,t}\). The central estimate is the posterior mean: \[ \hat{p}_{i,t} = \mathbb{E}[p_{i,t} \mid \text{Data}] \] We also construct 95% Bayesian credible intervals using the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the posterior distribution to represent model uncertainty.

title: Euro Area Recession Risk Indicator
text:
Welcome to the Euro Area Recession Risk Tracker. This page presents nowcasts of recession probabilities for the Euro Area (EA) and its four largest member states: Germany (DE), France (FR), Italy (IT), and Spain (ES).
Our methodology builds on the Bayesian logit nowcasting framework proposed by Furno and Giannone (2024). By utilizing a Hierarchical Bayesian model, we allow the model to share information across different regions. This hierarchical structure (“shrinkage”) is particularly valuable for improving the reliability of country-specific nowcasts during periods of high economic uncertainty. See Methodology for the full model specification.
Code
# The dashboard renders from the committed artifacts produced by
# new_code/update_dashboard_data.R (run on a host with RJSDMX/brms, e.g.
# production: DASHBOARD_PREDICTOR=esi Rscript --vanilla new_code/update_dashboard_data.R).
# It never downloads data or fits models here.

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(zoo)
library(scales)

data_dir <- file.path("..", "dashboard", "data")
if (!dir.exists(data_dir)) data_dir <- file.path("dashboard", "data")

esi_file <- file.path(data_dir, "probabilities_esi.csv")
pmi_file <- file.path(data_dir, "probabilities_pmi.csv")

# Default arm: ESI (public data). PMI is shown only if it is the only arm
# available; the backtest (new_code/pseudo_realtime_ESI_vs_PMI.R) decides
# which predictor to feature long-term.
if (file.exists(esi_file)) {
  arm <- "esi"
} else if (file.exists(pmi_file)) {
  arm <- "pmi"
} else {
  arm <- NULL
}

has_data <- !is.null(arm)

if (has_data) {
  probs <- read.csv(file.path(data_dir, paste0("probabilities_", arm, ".csv")),
                    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  meta <- read.csv(file.path(data_dir, paste0("meta_", arm, ".csv")),
                   stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

  probs$quarter <- as.yearqtr(probs$quarter, format = "%Y-Q%q")
  probs$geo <- factor(probs$geo, levels = c("EA", "DE", "FR", "IT", "ES"))

  cutoff_quarter <- as.yearqtr(meta$cutoff_quarter, format = "%Y-Q%q")
  max_quarter <- max(probs$quarter)
  window_start <- max_quarter - 10   # last 120 months (40 quarters)

  plot_df <- probs %>%
    filter(quarter >= window_start) %>%
    mutate(
      segment = factor(segment,
                       levels = c("in_sample", "out_of_sample", "nowcast")),
      is_nowcast = segment == "nowcast"
    )

  last_update <- format(as.POSIXct(meta$fitted_at_utc,
                                   tz = "UTC", tryFormats = c("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")),
                        "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M UTC")
}

title: Euro Area Recession Risk Indicator
text:
Dashboard Overview
The chart shows the estimated probability that each economy is in a technical recession (two consecutive quarters of negative quarter-on-quarter GDP growth). The model is trained on data up to the cutoff — five years before the latest available quarter — so the most recent five years are genuinely out-of-sample.

How to Read the Charts

Blue line (In-sample): model fit on the training window, shown for the first five years of the 10-year display window.
Orange line (Out-of-sample): model probabilities for the held-out last five years, computed with all currently available CISS and sentiment data.
Dashed orange line + dot (Nowcast): the extension beyond the last published GDP quarter — quarters whose three months of predictor data are already published but whose GDP outcome is not. This is the model’s current recession-risk reading; it becomes a verified out-of-sample point once GDP is released.
Grey shaded bars: quarters actually in a technical recession (ex-post, from published GDP).
Red dashed vertical line: the training cutoff (five years before the latest quarter).



Code
plot_geo <- function(data, region_name, is_main = FALSE) {
  p_data <- data %>% filter(geo == region_name)

  p <- ggplot(p_data, aes(x = zoo::as.Date(quarter))) +
    geom_rect(
      data = p_data %>% filter(recession_actual == 1),
      aes(xmin = zoo::as.Date(quarter) - 45,
          xmax = zoo::as.Date(quarter) + 45,
          ymin = 0, ymax = 1),
      fill = "grey80", alpha = 0.5, inherit.aes = FALSE
    ) +
    geom_ribbon(
      aes(ymin = lower_95, ymax = upper_95, fill = segment),
      alpha = 0.15, linetype = 0
    ) +
    geom_line(aes(y = prob_recession), colour = "grey75", linewidth = 0.5) +
    geom_line(
      data = p_data %>% filter(!is_nowcast),
      aes(y = prob_recession, colour = segment), linewidth = 1
    ) +
    geom_line(
      data = p_data %>% filter(is_nowcast),
      aes(y = prob_recession, colour = segment),
      linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed"
    ) +
    geom_point(
      data = p_data %>% filter(is_nowcast) %>% slice_tail(n = 1),
      aes(y = prob_recession), colour = "#E37222", size = 2
    ) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = zoo::as.Date(cutoff_quarter),
               linetype = "dashed", colour = "red") +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(), limits = c(0, 1)) +
    scale_x_date(breaks = pretty_breaks(6)) +
    scale_colour_manual(
      values = c("in_sample" = "#004B87", "out_of_sample" = "#E37222",
                 "nowcast" = "#E37222"),
      labels = c("In-sample (fit)", "Out-of-sample (last 5 yrs)",
                 "Nowcast (no GDP yet)")
    ) +
    scale_fill_manual(
      values = c("in_sample" = "#004B87", "out_of_sample" = "#E37222",
                 "nowcast" = "#E37222"),
      labels = c("In-sample (fit)", "Out-of-sample (last 5 yrs)",
                 "Nowcast (no GDP yet)")
    ) +
    labs(
      title = region_name,
      y = "Recession Probability", x = "",
      colour = NULL, fill = NULL
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
      legend.position = "bottom",
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold",
                                size = ifelse(is_main, 16, 12))
    )

  p
}

if (has_data) {
  p_ea <- plot_geo(plot_df, "EA", is_main = TRUE) +
    labs(subtitle = paste0(
      "Grey bars: actual technical recessions. Red dashed line: 5-year training cutoff. ",
      "Predictor: ", toupper(arm), " + CISS."
    ))
  p_de <- plot_geo(plot_df, "DE")
  p_fr <- plot_geo(plot_df, "FR")
  p_it <- plot_geo(plot_df, "IT")
  p_es <- plot_geo(plot_df, "ES")

  country_grid <- (p_de | p_fr) / (p_it | p_es) +
    plot_layout(guides = "collect") &
    theme(legend.position = "bottom")

  final_plot <- p_ea / country_grid + plot_layout(heights = c(1, 1.5))

  final_plot
} else {
  cat(
    "No dashboard artifacts found (dashboard/data/probabilities_*.csv).\n\n",
    "Generate them on a data host with:\n\n",
    "    DASHBOARD_PREDICTOR=esi Rscript --vanilla new_code/update_dashboard_data.R\n\n",
    "then re-render this site. See new_code/PROD_RUN_ESI_VS_PMI.md and the README.",
    sep = ""
  )
}

  paste0(
    "**Last updated**: ", last_update,
    "  \n**Training cutoff**: ", format(cutoff_quarter, "%Y Q%q"),
    "  \n**Latest model quarter**: ", format(max_quarter, "%Y Q%q"),

title: Euro Area Recession Risk Indicator
text:
Refreshing This Page
The page renders from committed CSV artifacts, so refreshing the forecast is a three-step cycle and never re-runs the model locally:

Update the data + fit (on a host with RJSDMX/brms, e.g. production): DASHBOARD_PREDICTOR=esi Rscript --vanilla new_code/update_dashboard_data.R
Commit the refreshed dashboard/data/probabilities_esi.csv and meta_esi.csv.
Render: make dashboard (or quarto render).

The PMI arm can be produced the same way with DASHBOARD_PREDICTOR=pmi (production only, see new_code/PROD_RUN_ESI_VS_PMI.md); the ESI-vs-PMI backtest decides which specification is featured here.

title: About
text: This site provides real-time monitoring and nowcasting of recession risk across the Euro Area and its main member states. The project is an empirical application and extension of the Bayesian nowcasting framework introduced by Furno and Giannone (2024).

title: About
text:
Data Sources
The model uses public macroeconomic and financial data retrieved directly from the APIs of official European statistical and financial institutions:

Gross Domestic Product (GDP)

Source: Eurostat API (Dataset: namq_10_gdp).
Definition: Quarter-on-Quarter percentage change of seasonally and calendar adjusted real Gross Domestic Product (market prices, B1GQ).
Role: Target variable for labeling technical recessions (defined as two consecutive quarters of negative growth).

Economic Sentiment Indicator (ESI)

Source: Eurostat API (Dataset: ei_bssi_m_r2).
Definition: Monthly composite index representing sentiment across industry, services, consumers, retail trade, and construction. The quarterly value is the simple average of the monthly indices in the quarter.
Role: Macroeconomic indicator representing economic activity expectations.

Composite Indicator of Systemic Stress (CISS)

Source: European Central Bank (ECB) Data Portal (Key: CISS.D..Z0Z.4F.EC.SS_CIN.IDX; the daily series is the only one disseminated on the SDMX API — the monthly key returns 404 — so the monthly/quarterly aggregates are computed from the daily index).
Definition: An index measuring systemic stress in the financial system. It aggregates segment-specific stress indices using portfolio theory to weight segments by their correlation, emphasizing joint stress events. The quarterly value is the average of the daily CISS values in the quarter.
Role: Financial stress indicator representing capital and credit risks.

title: About
text:
Model and Computation
The project is implemented in R and compiled via Quarto. The core statistical modeling relies on:

Bayesian Modeling: Estimated via Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) using the brms package, which runs on top of Stan.
Hierarchical Pooling: Intercepts and indicator coefficients (slopes) are modeled with group-level random effects grouped by geography (geo). This pools informational strength across countries to make predictions more robust.
Replicability: The R script recession-index.R downloads the latest data, fits the model, and displays the estimated probabilities; new_code/update_dashboard_data.R produces the persisted model artifacts consumed by the site.
